newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Peace to transform Guatemalan army.
newsitem.headline: Peace to transform Guatemalan army.

text.p: The Guatemalan army, which has dominated the nation's politics with a firm and bloody hand for decades, will become a shadow of its former self under the terms of a historic peace treaty being signed on Sunday.
"Next year is the year for big army transformations. We are ready for the restructuring," Defence Minister General Julio Balconi told Reuters in a recent interview.

Under an agreement reached in September between rebel forces and government peace negotiators, the 43,000-member army will shrink by a third, withdraw from five military zones, and abandon its internal security role.

The army has agreed to the changes as part of a political negotiation to end a conflict that dragged on despite the army's overwhelming superiority over a handful of leftist rebels from the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit.

On Sunday, rebel commanders will sign with President Alvaro Arzu a treaty ending the war, which is the most drawn-out conflict in Central America. A host of heads of state were due to attend the peace ceremony.
"I feel that cosmetically the army is washing its face now," former government peace negotiator Hector Rosada said.
"We have a weakened, wounded army that won militarily but lost all political power. They are like caged wild animals -- disoriented, discredited," he said.
According to Rosada, there is still a danger that extremist, hardline military factions could lash out violently in an attempt to destabilise peacetime Guatemala.
But army officers say that if hardliners had continued to wield any power, they would have stood up to Arzu in March when he suspended counterinsurgency operations.
Given Guatemala's history, fears of an extremist army backlash are not isolated.

For decades, with the backing of the right-wing business community, the Guatemalan army controlled every aspect of the country's political life, installing most presidents and staging a string of coups to impose dictators.
The army, often supported by U.S. funds and training, justified atrocities, torture, massacres and assassinations in the context of the Cold War.
Some 140,000 people died or were abducted and never seen again during the war, most at the hands of military and paramilitary groups seeking to snuff out rebel support.

Witnesses to massacres in rural villages during the height of the army's counterinsurgency efforts in the early 1980s have given gruesome accounts of soldiers run amok, burning down churches full of people and dismembering peasants.
Leftist congressman Amilcar Mendez called the army's legacy a "black history, black with crimes," and he said it continued to control parts of government, such as the judicial branch.
"The army has people all over, limiting judges from working freely and independently. The courts are saturated with army (intelligence) agents," Mendez said.
With the treaty to end 36 years of war, Defence Minister Balconi was confident that changes in the army were so profound that U.S. military aid would be resumed.

In the new environment of peace, Arzu has said Balconi could lose his position, his place taken by a civilian defence minister. Arzu also credits the army for not obstructing the peace process this year -- an acquiesence that surprised him.
Analysts said a gradual ideological shift among junior officers sickened by the army's reputation for brutality and backwardness may have helped push the institution toward supporting peace.
